papers.title: Outcomes of tracing antiretroviral therapy clients after missed clinic visits in South Africa: A retrospective cohort analysis
papers.abstract: Background In South Africa, interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) (missing a clinic visit or medication refill) for more than 28 days is very common, with an estimated 60% of clients interrupting at least once during their first year after initiation. Healthcare worker tracing of those who miss visits or medication refills, either through phone calls, text messages, or home visits (physical tracing), is a globally recommended, near-universal component of national HIV programs, but little is known about its effectiveness in returning clients to care. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of clients eligible for tracing under the South African national guidelines (7 or more days late for a scheduled visit) at 15 public-sector ART clinics between January 2024 and August 2025. Tracing records were abstracted from facility paper registers and linked to electronic medical records to determine outcomes. We report tracing contact status (reached directly, reached indirectly through family member or friend, not reached, unknown) and final outcomes (return to care, self-return, no return, transfer/death, misidentification), separately for telephone and physical tracing, including time to return to care using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results Tracing was attempted for 5,161 clients by telephone and 3,902 by physical visit. Roughly half of clients could be reached by tracers, either directly (43% telephone, 47% physical) or indirectly (7% telephone, 7% physical). Among those reached directly, 62-65% returned to care after contact. Among those who could not be reached, most nonetheless self-returned to care without any tracing contact (73% telephone, 65% physical), though more slowly than those who were reached. By day 90, two thirds of those reached directly by phone (68%) or physically (70%) had returned to care, compared to 60% and 53% of those not reached. Roughly 15% of tracing attempts targeted clients who had already returned to care, transferred, died, or had never actually interrupted care, reflecting data-quality challenges in the tracing and medical record systems. Conclusions Tracing HIV treatment clients who have missed clinic visits or medication pickups in South Africa appears to accelerate return to care but has an unclear effect on the overall proportion of those who return. Current data systems hamper efficient tracing efforts. Digitizing paper tracing registers, more targeted tracing that focuses limited resources on clients who genuinely require outreach, and interventions that promote client-initiated updates and two-way communication could allow better allocation of tracing resources to those truly in need.

papers.title: Distinct Systemic and Salivary Cytokine Profiles in Children with Perinatal HIV Exposure and Infection
papers.abstract: Background: Despite antiretroviral therapy (ART), children living with HIV (HI) experience a disproportionate burden of oral diseases, including dental caries. It remains unclear whether this increased susceptibility is associated with altered local expression of inflammatory cytokines, and whether systemic inflammatory profiles reflect corresponding immune signals in saliva. Methods: We analyzed 10 plasma and 7 salivary cytokines in matched plasma and unstimulated saliva samples from 467 Nigerian children aged 4-11 years: HI (n = 144), HEU (n = 161), and HUU (n = 162). Correlation analyses assessed plasma-saliva concordance, PERMANOVA evaluated overall cytokine profiles, multivariable linear regression examined individual cytokines, and network density analysis quantified connectivity. Results: Cytokines correlated more strongly within than between compartments. HIV exposure and infection status were associated with overall cytokine profiles in plasma (R^2 = 0.008, p = 0.038) and saliva (R^2 = 0.017, p < 0.001), and pairwise differences between comparison groups were significant only in saliva. HI children had higher plasma IL-5 and MCP-1 and higher salivary IL-6 and MCP-1 than HEU and HUU children. Higher CD4 T-cell count was associated with lower plasma IL-6 and MCP-1 and lower salivary IL-6. Caries status was not associated with overall cytokine profiles, but salivary IL-4 was higher in caries-free children. Conclusions: Plasma and salivary cytokines capture largely distinct immune signals in children affected by HIV, and saliva does not appear to serve as a surrogate for plasma with respect to cytokine expression. We did observe that HIV infection and immune status, not dental caries, were the main correlates of cytokine variation in plasma and saliva compartments.

papers.title: Retention in care and viral suppression among people on HIV treatment receiving 6- versus 12-month prescriptions in South Africa: a cohort study using routinely collected electronic health data
papers.abstract: Introduction During the COVID-19 pandemic, ART prescription lengths in South Africa were temporarily extended from six months to twelve months for stable clients, reducing required clinic visits from two to one per year. We compared retention and viral suppression outcomes between clients receiving 6-month and 12-month prescriptions within South Africa's Centralised Chronic Medicines Dispensing and Distribution (CCMDD) programme, which serves over 3.2 million people living with HIV through medication collection at facility-based or community-based pickup points. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in seven South African provinces using routinely collected electronic health data. We included adults ([≥]18) with a 6-month or 12-month ART prescription issued between June and November 2020. Participants were followed for 24 months. Retention was defined as [≥]1 medication collection visit during months 13-24 of follow-up and viral suppression as a viral load <50 copies/ml at the first test conducted in that window. We estimated unadjusted retention and suppression rates and then used a modified Poisson regression model with a log link and robust standard errors to compare non-retention and viral non-suppression between groups, accounting for district-level clustering and adjusting for age, sex, time on ART, model of care, and ART regimen. Results: Among 428,926 clients, 196,531 (46%) received 6-month prescriptions and 232,395 (54%) received 12-month prescriptions. During the outcome assessment period (months 13 to 24), clients in the 6-month group attended a median of 2 clinical prescribing visits and clients in the 12-month group attended a median of 1 clinical prescribing visit. Unadjusted retention was 91.4% in the 6-month group and 91.6% in the 12-month group; viral suppression was 79.3% in the 6-month group and 80.9% in the 12-month group. After adjustment, using the 6-month prescription group as the reference, adjusted risk ratios were 0.98 (0.91-1.05) for non-retention and 0.93 (0.82-1.06) for viral non-suppression. Conclusion: Twelve-month prescriptions maintained retention in care and viral suppression rates equal to 6-month prescriptions while halving required annual clinic visits per client. These findings support further evaluation of reduced-frequency prescribing within differentiated HIV service delivery programmes for stable clients and contribute to the evidence base to guide recommendations on reduced clinical prescribing visits.

papers.title: A COMPARISON OF TRENDS IN ADIPOSITY AND BLOOD PRESSURE AMONG PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV USING DOLUTEGRAVIR WITH OTHER ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPIES IN MWANZA TANZANIA
papers.abstract: Background: High blood pressure (BP) is a serious public health concern worldwide, including Tanzania, due to its impact in cardiovascular diseases. Among people living with HIV (PLHIV) high blood pressure has been linked with some anti-retroviral therapy (ART) regimens. Since its introduction in 2018, dolutegravir (DTG) has achieved a high rate of viral suppression compared to previous ART regimens. However, clinical and epidemiological studies have associated DTG with weight gain and other adiposity measures, which may increase the risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular diseases. Method: Between June 2016 and May 2021 500 adults PLHIV were started on ART, with BP, body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-height ratio (WtHR) measured at initiation and at regular follow-ups. Trends in BP, BMI, and WtHR were described using line graphs. Changes in BP, BMI and WtHR, and 95% confidence intervals (95%CI), associated with DTG or other ART regimes were assessed using mixed-effects linear regression models, with patients as clusters. Results: DTG was significantly associated with increase in BMI (coefficient=0.03, p=0.001, 95%CI=0.02-0.04) after adjusted for age and sex compared to other ART. DTG was not significantly associated with change in systolic BP compared with other ART regimens (coefficient=0.003, p=0.886, 95% CI:-0.04 to 0.05) after adjustment for BMI, age and sex. Conclusion: DTG was associated with greater increases in BMI compared to other ART regimens but after adjusting for BMI was not independently linked to higher systolic blood pressure. The absence of an association between DTG and SBP after adjustment for BMI suggests that differences in adiposity may partly account for the observed crude association.

papers.title: Integrated Stepped-Care Task-Shared Intervention for Depression Symptoms in Older Adults Living with HIV in Nigeria: A pilot randomized controlled study
papers.abstract: BackgroundDepression can affect treatment adherence and quality of life of older adults living with HIV, yet evidence on integrated stepped-care task-shared (SCT) interventions in African settings remains limited. We assessed the feasibility of an adapted SCT intervention among adults aged [≥]50 years receiving HIV care in Ibadan, Nigeria and examined preliminary differences in depressive symptoms, quality of life and ART adherence. MethodsThis was a two-arm, parallel-group, randomised pilot superiority trial embedded in a mixed-methods effectiveness-implementation study in Ibadan, Nigeria. Adults aged [≥]50 years living with HIV and scoring [≥]10 on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) were randomised (1:1) to stepped-care task-sharing (SCT; n=50) or treatment as usual (TAU; n=50). SCT involved psychosocial sessions delivered by trained HIV clinic providers, with antidepressant treatment and specialist review according to depression severity and treatment response. TAU involved routine HIV care and referral to a separate psychiatric clinic. Outcomes were assessed at six weeks, three months and six months by assessors blinded to allocation. Feasibility indicators included recruitment, retention and intervention delivery. Preliminary clinical effectiveness was assessed using mixed-effects models for PHQ-9, quality of life (WHOQOL-HIV BREF) and ART adherence (Simplified Medication Adherence Questionnaire). Analyses followed randomised allocation using Stata/MP 15. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06894680) ResultsOf the 757 participants screened, 120 participants were eligible and 100 (83.3%) were randomised, with 50 allocated to the SCT and 50 to TAU. All 50 SCT participants received the first psychosocial session, 40 (80%) attended at least two sessions and 30 (60%) completed all six sessions. Of 23 participants prescribed antidepressants, five (21.7%) initiated treatment. Baseline mean PHQ-9 scores were 13.24 (SD 4.43) in SCT and 14.12 (SD 4.48) in TAU. Of the 17 participants in TAU referred to the UCH psychiatric clinic, one attended but subsequently disengaged from care. Adjusted between-group differences (TAU minus SCT) favoured SCT at six weeks (3.95 points, 95% CI 1.91-5.99; p 0.05). Differences in quality of life and ART adherence were not statistically significant. No adverse events were recorded. ConclusionThis pilot trial demonstrated that the recruitment, retention and psychosocial SCT delivery were feasible within routine HIV care. SCT showed promising reductions in depressive symptoms over six months, although antidepressant initiation was limited. Further multisite evaluation should examine clinical effectiveness, intervention fidelity and implementation outcomes. Impact StatementDepression among older adults living with HIV can affect quality of life, treatment adherence, and overall well-being, yet mental health care is often not routinely integrated into HIV services, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study provides evidence on the feasibility of integrating a stepped-care, task-shared approach to depression management into existing HIV care and treatment in Nigeria. By involving non-specialist healthcare providers in delivering psychosocial support and facilitating access to specialist care when needed, the intervention offers a potentially practical approach to addressing the mental health needs of older adults without relying exclusively on scarce mental health professionals. The findings may inform the development and implementation of more accessible, sustainable, and integrated mental health services for ageing populations living with HIV in Nigeria and other similar settings. Ultimately, this research contributes to efforts to ensure that people ageing with HIV receive comprehensive care that addresses not only their physical health but also their mental health and quality of life.

papers.title: Does altering antiretroviral therapy impact an individual's gut microbiome?
papers.abstract: IntroductionPeople with HIV are living with increased chronic inflammation with gut microbiome dysbiosis and microbial translocation emerging as contributing factors to inflammation and development of HIV associated co-morbidities. Single time-point cross-sectional population studies of individuals on antiretroviral drug therapy have suggested that some classes of antiretroviral therapy (ART) affect the gut microbiome more than others. There is, however, a lack of data examining the microbiome changes prospectively in individuals before and after alteration of their antiretroviral regiment. This study prospectively assesses changes in individuals bacterial gut microbiome when switching from one antiretroviral drug or delivery method to another class or delivery method. MethodsWe conducted an observational prospective study of the gut microbiome in virologically controlled HIV infected individuals who were going through a planned switch of their ART regimen. We enrolled 15 participants and stool samples were collected before and 3-6 weeks after the switch of ART and analysed via shallow shotgun metagenomics. ResultsWe did not detect a statistically significant overall difference in microbiome perturbation between the study participant group that switched their antiretroviral therapy compared to the controls who continued with the same ART during the timeframe of the study. Though underpowered to detect changes in subgroups, a noticeable observational shift in the 20 most abundant bacterial species was seen when individuals changed from a protease inhibitor-based regime to a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) based regimen. Individuals who changed from NNRTI based treatment to integrase inhibitor-based treatment and from integrase inhibitor-based ART to protease inhibitor-based ART demonstrated numerical changes and shifts that failed to meet statistical significance. The initiation of intramuscular delivery of ART and a move away from oral drug did not result in a significant shift in the bacterial community in stool samples in this limited number of individuals. ConclusionWe did not see statistically significant changes that were larger than those observed in controls in this small study. Switching from protease inhibitor to NNRTI demonstrated the largest shift in bacterial species that had been previously associated with positive health outcomes, indicating that protease inhibitor-based regimen might have a negative effect on the gut microbiome. Further larger prospective studies are planned to explore this area.

papers.title: Understanding oral PrEP uptake and persistence among gay men and other men who have sex with men in Cape Town, South Africa: Perspectives of clients and providers
papers.abstract: BackgroundOral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is highly effective for preventing HIV acquisition when used consistently, but uptake and persistence remain suboptimal among gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in South Africa. We examined client and provider perspectives on PrEP uptake and persistence. MethodsBetween September and December 2022, we conducted three focus group discussions with 16 HIV-negative MSM eligible for, but not using, PrEP and six key informant interviews with PrEP providers at a specialized key population health clinic in Cape Town, South Africa. We analyzed transcripts thematically, using deductive codes informed by the PrEP cascade and the COM-B (capability, opportunity, motivation) model, plus inductive codes for emerging issues. ResultsFive themes emerged. Limited knowledge, misconceptions about PrEP and antiretroviral therapy, and low perceived risk reduced clients capability to make informed decisions about PrEP. HIV- and sexuality-related stigma, concerns about disclosure, and social surveillance were socially costly. Distance, transport costs, work commitments, clinic hours, and visit burden limited physical opportunity, whereas free care, short visits, reminders, and multi-month dispensing facilitated access. Daily pill-taking, side effects, forgetfulness, and changing sexual activity complicated persistence; routines, reminders, and acceptable PrEP modalities supported continued use. Non-judgmental, MSM-affirming services, counseling, and trusted providers fostered motivation by strengthening clients sense of safety, agency, and control. ConclusionPrEP delivery for MSM should extend beyond medication provision and address knowledge, stigma, service convenience, and motivation. Low-intensity adaptations, including tailored counseling, affirming care, flexible multi-month dispensing, and reminders, may improve uptake and persistence.

papers.title: Uptake and outcomes of earlier viral load testing and longer visit intervals in the early HIV treatment period: retrospective cohort analysis of South Africas 2023 ART guidelines revision
papers.abstract: South Africas 2023 revised ART Guidelines moved the first scheduled viral load (VL) test from 6 to 3 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and accelerated differentiated care eligibility from 7 to 4 months among virally suppressed clients. We assessed uptake of these changes and their association with virologic outcomes. We analysed routine electronic medical record data from 18 primary healthcare clinics in three South African districts among all adults initiating or re-initiating ART (N=16,338; January 2022-March 2025). Interrupted time series analyses were used to assess uptake of 3-month VL testing and assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals following guideline implementation in April 2023. Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days). At the first VL assessment, 27% of participants had VL tests at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; the rest had tests outside either window (19%) or no test documented (25%). Three-month VL testing rose immediately after guideline implementation, reaching 72-85% coverage by the end of the study period. Assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals among clients with 3-month viral suppression increased after implementation, reaching 48-71% across districts. A second VL result was documented for 62% of clients tested in the 3- or 6-month window. Viral suppression did not differ meaningfully between clients initially tested at 3 months (72%) and those initially tested at 6 months (72%). Among clients with a second scheduled VL result, 82% were virally suppressed. Assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals was not associated with subsequent viral suppression (aRR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.06). Results should be interpreted with caution due to missing VL data. South Africas 2023 guideline revision was associated with rapid increases in 3-month VL testing and assignment to longer visit intervals. Viral suppression at the first VL test was similar among clients tested at 3 and 6 months, and longer visit intervals were not associated with poorer outcomes. These findings support earlier differentiation of HIV care within routine service delivery. Incomplete uptake of recommended testing and visit intervals offers opportunities to strengthen implementation and warrants continued evaluation of longer-term outcomes.

papers.title: Determinants of Condom Use Among Sexually Active Men in a High-HIV-Burden Municipality in Ghana
papers.abstract: Consistent and correct condom use remains one of the most effective strategies for preventing sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, yet the determinants of male condom use are poorly documented at the district level in Ghana. This mixed-methods, cross-sectional study examined individual, sociocultural, and environmental determinants of condom use among 314 sexually active men aged 15 to 59 years, surveyed in 2016 in the Lower Manya Krobo Municipality, a district with historically elevated HIV prevalence (11.6% in 2013, 5.56% in 2019, and 4.65% in 2024). Data were collected via a structured questionnaire and focus group discussions with eight participants. In the final multivariable logistic regression model, having children was the only factor independently associated with ever having used a condom (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 95% confidence interval 1.74 to 6.19, p<0.001); age group, marital status, community of residence, and religion are not reported as adjusted estimates because their values were unstable in the presence of sparse cells. In the focus group discussions, younger men described pregnancy prevention rather than disease avoidance as their main motivation for condom use, while religious belief and social stigma (55.4% agreeing condom use is immoral, 58.3% citing partner-suspicion stigma) emerged as persistent barriers to acceptability. A gap between high awareness of condom effectiveness (77.1%) and frequent self-reported slippage or breakage (65.2% of ever-users) suggested a skills rather than a knowledge deficit. Although the data are a decade old, the normative and religious barriers recur in more recent national surveys, and the district remains comparatively high-burden, suggesting continued programmatic relevance. HIV and STI prevention programming for Ghanaian men may be more effective when framed within a broader sexual and reproductive health and family-planning context. Engaging religious and community leaders directly and incorporating hands-on condom-use skills training rather than risk-based knowledge messaging alone may be effective.

papers.title: Prevalence and risk factors for human papillomavirus infection among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone: A cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCervical cancer, a malignancy affecting the cervix, is the fourth most common cancer and cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. This burden disproportionately affects low-resource regions, where approximately 90% of cases occur. HIV-positive women are at high risk of persistent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical cancer, but screening for this cancer is not yet integrated into HIV care in Sierra Leone. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and risk factors of high-risk HPV infection among women living with HIV (WLHIV) attending Connaught Hospital in Sierra Leone. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study of women living with HIV aged 25-65 years attending the HIV clinic at Connaught Teaching Hospital in Freetown between September and December 2024. Endocervical swabs were collected for HPV DNA testing. Data was analyzed using R (v4.4.0). Logistic regression analysis was used to determine the independent risk factors for HPV positivity. ResultsA total of 191 WLHIV were enrolled. The mean age was 36.8 years; 44.5% were single, and 67% were employed. High-risk HPV DNA was detected in 60 (31.4%) (95% CI 25.3%-38.3%) participants, with 50% (30/60) having multiple serotypes. The most common genotype was HPV 52, followed by 16 and 51. Only 30% of HPV-positive women had genotypes 16 or 18, targeted by the bivalent vaccine. On multivariable analysis, former contraceptive use was independently associated with increased HPV positivity (aOR=4.86, 95% CI: 1.65-17.37, p = 0.0032). ConclusionThe high prevalence of high-risk HPV infection and predominance of non 16/18 genotypes among WLHIV in Sierra Leone underscore the need to integrate HPV screening within HIV services and consider broader HPV vaccine coverage in Sierra Leone. Former contraceptive use is an independent predictor of HPV positivity, emphasizing the need for robust screening strategies in women using contraceptives.

papers.title: Investigating Biological Aging Measures, Neurocognitive Performance, and Depressive Symptoms: Moderating Effects of HIV and Childhood Maltreatment
papers.abstract: IntroductionNeurocognitive impairment and depression remain common among people with HIV (PWH), and childhood maltreatment (CM) may further increase vulnerability. In this cohort, we previously reported that PWH exhibited shorter absolute telomere length, lower MRI- based brain-predicted age difference, and greater epigenetic age acceleration (AA) compared to controls, with limited associations with CM severity. Building on this, the present study examines whether these markers are linked to neurocognitive performance and depressive symptoms, and whether HIV status or CM severity moderates such associations. MethodsIn this study of 238 women (122 PWH), biological aging was assessed using absolute telomere length, mitochondrial DNA copy number, MRI-based brain-predicted age difference, and DNA methylation AA measures, including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, Horvath intrinsic epigenetic, and Hannum intrinsic epigenetic and extrinsic epigenetic AA. Neurocognitive performance was measured using a standardised assessment battery and global deficit scores (GDS) were derived. Depressive symptoms were assessed with the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies - Depression Scale. Linear regression models examined associations with GDS and depressive symptoms, with interaction models evaluating moderation by HIV status and CM severity. ResultsBiological aging markers were not associated with either neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms. Though HIV infection in combination with higher mitochondrial DNA copy number and extrinsic epigenetic AA was nominally associated with higher GDS (p = 0.012 and p = 0.047, respectively), these associations did not survive correction for multiple testing. Neither HIV nor CM moderated the association between biological aging markers and depression scores. ConclusionsDespite accelerated biological aging being evident in PWH, we found limited evidence of association with neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms, underscoring their multifactorial nature. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these markers predict neurocognitive and psychiatric trajectories.

papers.title: Diagnosis Journey and Future Outlook Among Young People Living with HIV in Bangladesh: protocol for a qualitative study
papers.abstract: IntroductionBangladesh is a country with low HIV prevalence, but case detection has more than doubled in 2020- 24, reaching 1,891 cases in the most recently reported year, and the number of cases is growing in the 18-24 age group. There is little qualitative evidence that describes the journey from suspected exposure to diagnosis for young people in Bangladesh, and no comparative evidence of this journey between key-population and general-population youth. ObjectiveTo explore the pathway to HIV testing and diagnosis, what motivated testing, and the life outlook of people living with HIV in Bangladesh aged 18-30 years, and to compare these between key-population and general-population participants. MethodsThis qualitative exploratory study uses semi-structured in-depth interviews, guided by the theory of emerging adulthood and the HIV Stigma Framework. Purposive maximum-variation sampling (20-30 participants) will recruit people aged 18-30, diagnosed within that age range and currently on antiretroviral therapy, balanced between key and general populations. Participants will be recruited through Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and Ashar Alo Society, Dhaka, and interviewed privately in Bangla. Recordings will be transcribed, translated into English, and analysed with the Framework Method in MAXQDA, with saturation judged within each group. Ethical concernsThe study is approved by the Ethical Review Board, Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Dhaka with written consent from Ashar Alo Society and PLHIV Network Bangladesh. All participants will be asked for written informed consent, identifiers will be removed and distressed participants will be referred for counselling and psychosocial support. Findings will be shared via a technical report, a policy brief for the National AIDS/STD Programme and partner organisations, conference presentations and peer-reviewed publication. LimitationsThe recruitment process via one gatekeeper organisation in Dhaka and the need for the participants to be on treatment may exclude young people not in care. (300 words)

papers.title: Sex, age and HIV-1 status influence complement activation against SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine Spike protein
papers.abstract: Regulation of complement activity influences immunity and clinical outcomes of SARS-CoV-2 infections. Here we investigated antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and complement activity in men (age 36 to 86) and women (age 39 to 83) with (MWH, WWH) and without (MWOH, WWOH) HIV-1. Antibody responses in WWH were lower than in MWH. WWH also had negligible change in blood C3a post-immunization, whereas MWH had greater C3a levels. We investigated the levels of C5, C5a, C1-INH, factor H, and circulating immune complex-C1q (CIC-C1q) binding to understand the regulation of complement activity. We found that C1-INH and anti-S antibody levels were driving the differences in C3 convertase activity in MWH. No significant differences were found between C5 and C5a in both cohorts, suggesting that C5 convertase is not being activated. These results show that biological sex may impact SARS-CoV-2 immune responses and highlights the need for further investigation.

papers.title: Syndemic burden, menopause, and cardiovascular risk among midlife and older women with and without HIV
papers.abstract: Midlife and older women living with HIV often carry several co-occurring social and behavioral stressors, and how that accumulated burden relates to cardiovascular risk is not well described. We examined whether cumulative syndemic burden was associated with estimated 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease among women aged 45 years and older, and whether menopause stage modified it. Data came from the MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study, a multisite United States cohort, for visits between October 2020 and March 2025. The full sample included 1,993 women, 1,446 of them living with HIV; a secondary sample of 1,063 women virally suppressed at baseline contributed 4,009 visits. Syndemic burden was the sum of six conditions: elevated depressive symptoms, current tobacco use, hazardous alcohol use, recent stimulant use, physical inactivity, and material insecurity. Ten-year cardiovascular risk was estimated with the Pooled Cohort Equations and modeled with linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts; random forest classifiers were trained separately to predict high estimated risk (7.5 percent or greater). Median age was 56 years, 63 percent were non-Hispanic Black, and 57 percent reported two or more syndemic conditions. Each additional syndemic condition was associated with a 0.40-point higher estimated risk score (95 percent confidence interval 0.01 to 0.78; p=0.043), and postmenopausal status with a 1.3-point higher score than premenopause (0.39 to 2.3; p=0.006). The syndemic burden by menopause stage interaction was not significant overall (p=0.2), although an exploratory signal was present among virally suppressed women (0.50; p=0.079). The classifiers discriminated moderately (areas under the curve 0.727 and 0.704); serum creatinine, body mass index, syndemic burden, and postmenopausal status ranked among the most important predictors. Syndemic burden and reproductive aging were each independently and modestly associated with higher estimated cardiovascular risk, supporting joint assessment of both in risk stratification for midlife women with and without HIV.

papers.title: Structural and Social Disadvantage and Post-Migration HIV Vulnerability among African, Caribbean, and Black Communities in Ontario
papers.abstract: BackgroundAfrican, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities in Canada experience a disproportionate burden of HIV, and a considerable share of infections among ACB immigrants is acquired after arrival in Canada. Yet how ACB people themselves understand the structural circumstances surrounding post-migration acquisition remains underexamined. This study asked how intersecting structural and social disadvantages shape post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities in Ontario. MethodsWe conducted an interpretive secondary thematic analysis of 44 in-depth interviews from the MSAFIRI Study, read through intersectionality and structural-vulnerability lenses. Interviews were coded inductively and deductively by two analysts, with consensus adjudication and community review of the thematic structure. ResultsFive structural conditions organized participants accounts: racism as a structural condition of settlement; immigration precarity and the work of settling alone; economic precarity, including insecure work, poverty, and unstable housing; ruptured kin networks and isolation under migration; and gendered violence and homophobia. These conditions compounded one another, so that disadvantage in one domain deepened vulnerability in another. Conclusion. Post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities is produced by intersecting structural disadvantages encountered in the receiving country context. Equitable HIV prevention requires structural and community-led responses that address immigration precarity, economic and housing insecurity, gendered violence, homophobia, and anti-Black racism, alongside biomedical and individual-level prevention.

papers.title: Stigma, Place, and HIV: The Legacy of the 1984 Bhopal Gas Disaster Among Indian Men Who Have Sex with Men
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe 1984 Bhopal Gas Leak is widely considered the worst industrial disaster in history, and "big events" can have durable impacts on infectious disease transmission. Among men who have sex with men, we examined whether meeting sexual partners near the original gas leak site was associated with HIV, HIV-associated risk behaviors, and sexual stigma. MethodsWe used respondent-driven sampling to enroll MSM in Bhopal during 2023-24 (n=750). Participants reported the four locations where they most often went to meet sexual partners in the past year. Sexual stigma was defined by mechanism (enacted, anticipated, internalized) and source (healthcare, family, society). We calculated weighted (RDS-II) prevalences of HIV, population-level HIV viremia ([≥]200 copies/ml), and associated risk behaviors by meeting location type and distance to the original gas leak site. We used weighted logistic regression to examine associations between sexual stigma and partner meeting locations. ResultsHIV prevalence was elevated among participants meeting near the leak site: 21.7% within 1 km, 14.4% between 1-2 km, and 9.7% over 2 km. Population-level HIV viremia and the proportion of MSM engaging in sex work were also elevated within 2 km. Sexual stigma measures were significantly associated with meeting a partner within 2 km of the leak site. Transportation-related spaces were associated with higher prevalences of HIV and viremia. ConclusionsIndustrial disasters may create marginal spaces which concentrate individuals facing greater stigma and elevated HIV transmission risk. Venue-based interventions near the gas leak site and at transportation centers may be warranted in Bhopal. FundingThis study was supported by the National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01DA041034. GJB, CC, and TL were supported by National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases grant T32AI102623. SJC was funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DP2DA056130. SSS was funded by National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DP1DA060602.

papers.title: Global Disparities in Vaccine Reimbursement for Adults Living with HIV: A Cross-Sectional Survey of 120 Countries
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAdults living with HIV are at increased risk of vaccine-preventable infections, yet access to recommended vaccines varies globally. We evaluated national vaccination guidelines, public reimbursement, and on-site vaccination availability across countries with different income levels. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional survey of HIV clinicians and experts representing 120 countries. The 26-item questionnaire assessed vaccination guidelines, recommendations, public reimbursement, and on-site vaccination availability. Countries were classified according to World Bank income group. Generalized linear mixed-effects models assessed routine recommendations, full reimbursement, and recommendation-reimbursement gaps by vaccine type and income group. ResultsA total of 124 responses representing 120 countries were analyzed, including 38 low-/lower-middle-income (LIC/LMIC), 36 upper-middle-income (UMIC), and 50 high-income countries (HIC). HIV-specific national vaccination guidelines were reported by 37% of respondents, increasing from 18% in LIC/LMIC to 52% in HIC (p=0.026). Only 30% reported full public reimbursement for all recommended vaccines (13% LIC/LMIC, 28% UMIC, 44% HIC;p=0.007). Mixed-effects analyses showed significant differences in routine recommendations and full reimbursement by vaccine type and income group. The adjusted probability of routine recommendation was lower in LIC/LMIC than HIC countries (52.6% vs 77.6%; adjusted p=0.0013). Among recommended vaccines, more than 94% of influenza, pneumococcal, and hepatitis B vaccinations lacked full reimbursement in LIC/LMIC, based on adjusted estimates. Reimbursement gaps for HPV and herpes zoster vaccines remained substantial even in HIC. On-site vaccination was also less available in LIC/LMIC than in HIC (55% vs 78%; p=0.020). ConclusionsSignificant income-related disparities persist in vaccination policy and implementation for adults living with HIV. Gaps between recommendations and financial access are particularly pronounced in lower-income settings, while HPV and herpes zoster reimbursement remains limited across all income groups. Expanding HIV-specific vaccination policies, improving public reimbursement, and integrating vaccination into routine HIV services are essential to improve access to recommended vaccines for this population.

papers.title: Postnatal CMV acquisition risk is not increased among children who are HIV-exposed, uninfected versus HIV-unexposed in the setting of optimized maternal ART
papers.abstract: Historically, children who are HIV-exposed, uninfected (CHEU) had higher incidence and earlier postnatal acquisition of cytomegalovirus (CMV) than children who are HIV-unexposed. We assessed whether this difference persists in the current era of universal antiretroviral therapy (ART). Women without HIV and women living with HIV (WLHIV) on ART for [≥]6 months were recruited in pregnancy in Nairobi, Kenya and followed weekly with their infant for 12 months postpartum; 89% of WLHIV initiated ART pre-conception. Log10-CMV DNA levels were measured in infant urine, oral swabs, and plasma, and in maternal breast milk, oral swabs, and vaginal swabs. Infant plasma collected at age [≥]12 months was tested for CMV IgG antibodies. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression were used to compare CMV acquisition by HIV exposure and assess correlates of CMV infection. Of 65/72 (90%) infants with ascertainable CMV status and timing of acquisition (42% CHEU), 47 (72%) acquired CMV. WLHIV had higher mean CMV DNA levels than women without HIV in breast milk (4.17-log vs 3.12-log, p<0.001) and oral swabs (1.10-log vs 0.78-log, p<0.001). Though higher breast milk and oral swab CMV DNA levels were associated with increased hazard of CMV among all infants (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]=2.80, 95% CI: 1.77-4.43 and aHR=1.35, 95% CI: 1.14-1.60), HIV exposure was not significantly associated with CMV acquisition (aHR=1.31, 95% CI: 0.71-2.42). Hazard of CMV was lower among CHEU that received cotrimoxazole prophylaxis (aHR=0.19, 95% CI: 0.074-0.47) and whose mothers received a recommended first line ART regimen postpartum (aHR=0.37, 95% CI: 0.15-0.93). Together, these findings suggest that risk of CMV infection among CHEU is modulated by level of maternal mucosal CMV shedding, maternal ART regimen, and cotrimoxazole in this setting of optimized, pre-conception ART. Breast milk remains an important source of postnatal CMV acquisition for all infants.

papers.title: Psychological inoculation protects young women in South Africa against HIV prevention misinformation: Evidence from a randomised controlled trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundMisinformation decreases public confidence in health technologies and willingness to use them. Psychological inoculation, or "prebunking", exposes people to misleading claims before they spread widely and refutes the claims and embedded persuasion tactics. Evidence on its effectiveness for HIV-related misinformation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and among young women (a population highly vulnerable to HIV), is limited. MethodsWe conducted a randomised controlled trial (July to October 2025) among 2,163 women aged 18-29 years recruited online in South Africa. Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes. All participants then viewed multiple false claims presented as social media posts. The primary outcome was intention to receive an HIV vaccine if available (1-10 scale), assessed immediately post-intervention and at three-week follow-up. Secondary outcomes included likelihood of recommending the vaccine; and perceived credibility, emotional impact, and shareability of misinformation claims. We used linear regression models to estimate intervention effects. ResultsMisinformation exposure reduced vaccine intentions by 0.63 points in the control group, while intentions increased by 0.30 points in the intervention group. Controlling for covariates and baseline intentions, post-exposure vaccine intentions were 0.92 points higher in the intervention group (95% CI 0.78, 1.06; p<0.01), a 12% relative increase. Intervention participants were also more likely to recommend the vaccine (+0.74; 95% CI 0.61, 0.88; p<0.01). Inoculation reduced perceived credibility, emotional distress, and sharing intentions across all false claims. Effects persisted at three-week follow-up (vaccine intentions: +0.97; 95% CI 0.78, 1.17; p<0.01). ConclusionBrief, scalable psychological inoculation delivered via social-media-style videos protected young womens HIV vaccine intentions, with effects generalising to novel claims and persisting over three weeks. Prebunking campaigns may safeguard public confidence in other new HIV prevention technologies like lenacapavir.

papers.title: HIV-related knowledge and sexual decision-making indicators among Kenyan boys aged 11-14 years who had heard of HIV: A secondary analysis of the 2018 Kenya Population-based HIV Impact Assessment.
papers.abstract: Adolescents remain a priority population in HIV prevention efforts in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet, evidence on the relationship between HIV knowledge and sexual decision-making indicators among boys in early adolescence in Kenya is limited. This study examined the association between HIV-related knowledge and intention to have sex before marriage, perceived ability to refuse unwanted sex, and communication with a parent or guardian about sex among Kenyan boys aged 11-14 years who reported knowing what sex was and having heard of HIV. We conducted a secondary cross-sectional analysis of data from the Kenya Population-based HIV Impact Assessment 2018-2019 (KENPHIA), a nationally representative household survey. The analysis was restricted to boys aged 11-14 years who participated in the child survey, completed the interview, had a valid survey weight, reported knowing what sex is, and had heard of HIV, resulting in a final analytic sample of 495 participants from 1,024 boys who completed the child questionnaire and had valid survey weights. HIV-related knowledge was assessed using a study-specific index derived from five knowledge items and grouped as 0-2, 3-4, or 5 correct responses. The outcomes were intention to have sex before marriage (n = 408), perceived ability to refuse unwanted sex (n = 479), and communication with a parent or guardian about sex (n = 495). Survey-weighted Poisson regression models with a log link and jackknife variance estimation were used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Models were adjusted for age, education level, and residence. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by modeling the HIV knowledge score as a continuous variable. After adjustment for age, residence, and education, HIV-related knowledge categories were not associated with intention to have sex before marriage. Compared with boys with 0-2 correct responses, those with 3-4 or all five correct responses were more likely to report being able to refuse unwanted sex, although prevalence did not rise further in the five-correct group (aPR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.11-1.57; aPR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.06-1.57, respectively). Parent/guardian communication prevalence rose across knowledge categories, but category-specific associations were not statistically significant. In sensitivity analyses, each additional correct response was associated with perceived ability to refuse unwanted sex (aPR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02-1.14) and parent/guardian communication (aPR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.03-1.60), but not with intention to have sex before marriage. However, the association for perceived refusal ability departed from linearity. Among Kenyan boys aged 11-14 years who reported knowing what sex is and having heard of HIV, greater HIV-related knowledge was associated with a higher prevalence of perceived ability to refuse unwanted sex but not with intention to have sex before marriage. Findings for parent/guardian communication differed between the categorical and continuous specifications of the knowledge score and should be interpreted cautiously. Age-specific HIV prevention approaches that combine knowledge with communication, life-skills, safeguarding, and social support interventions warrant prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Factors Influencing Timely Utilization of HIV Viral Load Test Results in HIV Care: A Qualitative Study at Kisenyi Health Centre IV, Kampala
papers.abstract: Structured AbstractTimely utilization of HIV viral load (VL) test results is critical for effective monitoring of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and achieving viral suppression among people living with HIV. However, delays in utilizing VL results remain a challenge in many resource-limited settings. This study explored the factors influencing timely utilization of VL test results at Kisenyi Health Centre IV in Kampala, Uganda. A qualitative study design was employed using key informant interviews and structured facility observations. Eighteen healthcare workers involved in HIV care and viral load management participated in the study, including clinicians, laboratory personnel, data clerks, counsellors, and facility management staff. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and observation checklists. Interview transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis guided by the Performance of Routine Information System Management (PRISM) Framework. Three major themes emerged: technical, behavioral, and organizational factors. Technical barriers included unstable digital systems, limited computer access, unreliable internet connectivity, and fragmented health information platforms that delayed result retrieval. Behavioral factors included workload pressures, training gaps, and varying levels of staff motivation and accountability. Organizational challenges included staffing shortages, weak supervision, inconsistent feedback mechanisms, and occasional stock-outs of printing materials. Observational findings confirmed that manual printing and re-entry of VL results into electronic systems contributed to delays in clinical decision-making. Timely utilization of viral load results is influenced by a combination of technical, behavioral, and organizational factors. Strengthening digital system integration, improving health worker capacity, and enhancing facility-level management support could significantly improve VL result utilization and HIV treatment outcomes.

papers.title: Cross-national factors associated with governmental responses to the 2025 PEPFAR funding freeze
papers.abstract: Since its inception in 2003, the United States Presidents Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) has played a central role in HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment across Sub-Saharan Africa. Following the January 2025 suspension of United States foreign aid, which includes PEPFAR funding, countries across Sub-Saharan Africa demonstrated varying governmental responses to the resulting HIV funding disruptions. This study evaluates whether national characteristics were associated with a countrys ability to respond to this funding crisis. Countries in Sub-Saharan Africa receiving PEPFAR funding were classified into one of three response categories: Level 1 (minimal or no governmental response), Level 2 (government response without sufficient plans or resources to fully offset funding losses), or Level 3 (high governmental response with strategies to maintain HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment services). Response categories were compared with national Human Development Index (HDI), GDP per capita, HIV prevalence, total population living with HIV, annual HIV mortality, and historical PEPFAR funding. Univariable proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with response level. Five countries (17.2%) were classified as Level 1, 10 (34.5%) as Level 2, and 14 (48.3%) as Level 3. Higher HDI was significantly associated with stronger governmental response (OR = 4.05; 95% CI, 1.49-11.04; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0376). GDP per capita (OR = 2.35; 95% CI, 1.00-5.51; unadjusted p = 0.0489) and HIV prevalence (OR = 3.53; 95% CI, 1.03-12.11; unadjusted p = 0.0452) demonstrated positive associations before adjustment for multiple comparisons, but neither remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.2261 for both). Historical PEPFAR funding, total population living with HIV, and annual HIV mortality were not significantly associated with response level after adjustment. Countries with higher levels of human development demonstrated stronger governmental responses to the 2025 PEPFAR funding disruptions. Several countries with minimal documented responses were also affected by active conflict or political instability, potentially compounding their vulnerability to treatment interruptions. These findings suggest that broader national development may play an important role in governmental responses to funding disruptions and highlight the need to strengthen resilient health systems, diversify HIV financing, and prioritize support for countries at greatest risk of future funding shocks.

papers.title: Assessing the Competing Risks of Loss to Follow-up and Mortality Among Adults Receiving Antiretroviral Therapy in Northern Ghana: Application of the Fine-Gray Subdistribution Hazard Model
papers.abstract: BackgroundRetention in antiretroviral therapy (ART) programmes remains a major public health challenge in HIV care, with loss to follow-up (LTFU) and death threatening treatment success. Because these outcomes are competing events, conventional survival methods may yield biased estimates of their incidence and associated risk factors. ObjectiveTo estimate the cumulative incidence of LTFU and mortality and identify factors associated with these outcomes among adults receiving ART in Northern Ghana using a competing-risks framework. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of 329 adults living with HIV who initiated ART at Nalerigu Baptist Medical Centre, Ghana, between January 2013 and December 2019. Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models were used to evaluate predictors of LTFU and death while accounting for competing risks. Cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models were fitted as a sensitivity analysis. ResultsThe incidence rates were 2.2 per 100 person-months (95% CI: 1.9-2.6) for LTFU and 0.74 per 100 person-months (95% CI: 0.57-0.98) for death. At 36 months, the cumulative incidence was 50.2% for LTFU and 16.0% for death. Patients residing closer to the clinic had a lower cumulative incidence of LTFU than those living farther away (SHR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.49-0.93), whereas higher baseline weight was associated with increased LTFU (SHR = 1.02 per kg, 95% CI: 1.00-1.04). Mortality was lower among patients receiving efavirenz-based regimens (SHR = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.15-0.50), females (SHR = 0.39, 95% CI: 0.18-0.85), and those with higher baseline weight (SHR = 0.93 per kg, 95% CI: 0.90-0.96). Findings were broadly consistent in cause-specific Cox models. ConclusionLTFU was substantially more frequent than mortality among adults receiving ART in Northern Ghana. Travel distance to the treatment facility was an important barrier to retention, while ART regimen, sex, and baseline weight were associated with mortality. Expanding access to ART services through decentralized and community-based models may improve retention and support efforts to achieve HIV control targets.

papers.title: Combining Randomized and Observational Data: The Case of Postnatal Prophylaxis Against HIV
papers.abstract: The efficacy of current antiretroviral interventions for prevention of vertical HIV transmission is both a triumph and a challenge for future efficacy studies of novel agents, including long-acting antiretroviral agents. Given the effectiveness of current antiretroviral interventions, standard randomized controlled trials to assess novel interventions targeted towards further reducing vertical HIV transmission may be infeasible due to required sample sizes. To address this study design challenge, we propose a novel augmented clinical trial design, where a randomized trial with an active comparator is augmented with a concurrent observational cohort to supplement the standard-of-care arm. The proposed design and analysis can overcome sampling biases, and an associated diagnostic can evaluate potential biases from unmeasured covariates. The proposed trial design is illustrated with an example and studied further using a simulation study. In the illustrative example, an augmented trial with a 3:1 allocation ratio in the trial component yielded an unbiased treatment effect estimate, as compared to the trial component alone, and the standard error was reduced substantially. Although the total sample size of the augmented trial was larger than a similarly powered 1:1 standard trial, the sample size of the augmented trials trial component was half the size of the standard trial and within the range of historically similar trials, thereby providing both feasibility and potential cost advantages. Although limitations with this design remain, many of these limitations can be mitigated by careful study planning and coordination. Augmented trials provide a potentially applicable solution to studying the efficacy of long-acting antiretrovirals for infant postnatal prophylaxis against HIV.

papers.title: Biological aging markers in South African women with HIV and variable exposure to childhood maltreatment
papers.abstract: IntroductionHIV and childhood maltreatment (CM) are both chronic stressors that disproportionately affect women, with each contributing to accelerated biological aging. Whether biological aging markers are convergent and associate with HIV and CM is unclear. MethodsWe studied 238 women (122 with HIV), characterised for CM severity, and assessed biological aging using absolute telomere length (aTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNAcn), magnetic resonance imaging-based brain-predicted age difference (MRI-BPAD), and DNA methylation age (DNAmAge) clocks. CM was measured with the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form total score. We examined intercorrelations among biological aging markers to assess convergence and conducted linear regression models to test moderation by HIV status and CM severity. ResultsPWH had shorter aTL, lower MRI-BPAD, and higher Horvath age acceleration (HorvathAA), HannumAA, PhenoAA, and extrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (EEAA). CM had limited associations with biological aging markers. Absolute TL correlated weakly with mtDNAcn ({rho} = 0.36), PhenoAA ({rho} = -0.18), and EEAA ({rho} = -0.18), while MRI-BPAD correlated weakly with PhenoAA (r = 0.20). DNAmAge clocks were moderately to strongly intercorrelated (r = 0.35 - 0.93). No robust two- or three-way moderation effects were observed after false discovery rate correction. ConclusionOur findings support a multidimensional pattern of biological aging, with substantial convergence among epigenetic aging measures but limited relationships across different markers, largely independent of HIV status and CM severity. Longitudinal approaches are needed to clarify how distinct biological aging markers relate to one another and to health outcomes over time in vulnerable populations.

papers.title: Mechanisms of action of a community-led HIV prevention and treatment programme for female sex workers in Zimbabwe: a mixed-method analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundCommunity-led interventions for female sex workers (FSW) can improve HIV prevention and treatment outcomes by lowering self-stigma and strengthening social cohesion to improve service uptake. In Zimbabwe, the AMETHIST intervention trial integrated peer-led microplanning with self-help groups for FSW and demonstrated improved HIV treatment outcomes. We investigated the role of social cohesion and self-stigma in explaining these findings. MethodWe conducted a mixed-method analysis of data collected during AMETHIST. We re-analysed qualitative data from interviews and group discussions to identify narratives linking self-stigma, engagement with microplanners and/or self-help groups and HIV service use. We analysed quantitative data from endline respondent-driven sampling surveys for differences in self-reported measures of social cohesion and self-stigma between trial arms, and between those who did and did not participate in intervention activities or access services. ResultsIn both arms, FSW self-reported engaging with peer supporters, participating in self-help groups and accessing HIV services. Qualitative narratives suggested peer support and group participation could reduce self-stigma and support service uptake. Lower levels of self-stigma were seen in the intervention arm (58.6% vs 63.2%; aOR 0.77; 95% CI 0.61-0.86). Social cohesion exceeded 50% across the whole sample, but was not associated with study arm, nor with engagement in intervention-related activities. DiscussionAlthough qualitative data suggested some FSW felt their uptake of services was influenced by intervention components, quantitative analyses did not suggest either variable was on the causal pathway to the outcomes of the intervention. A limitation may have been the measurement of these complex constructs and the high levels of social cohesion across both study arms. Contributions to the literature- Community-led, empowerment-based interventions are the cornerstone of effective HIV responses for sex workers. The hypothesised mechanisms of improved social cohesion and self-efficacy through which these work to increase HIV services uptake are less well understood. - Our study contributes to evidence on the social mechanisms through which community based interventions work to improve HIV outcomes among female sex workers in Zimbabwe - Our study found that female sex workers who more frequently accessed HIV services were more likely to report higher levels of social cohesion, but was unable to establish whether this was a mechanism along the pathway between intervention engagement and improved HIV outcomes Our study indicated that reductions in self-stigma through peer-led community-based support are important for HIV programme implementation; increasing the uptake of HIV services and improving HIV outcomes

papers.title: Readiness to start long acting injectable HIV treatment and prevention and conditions for acceptance among clinic clients in Uganda
papers.abstract: Long-acting injectable human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) medicines expand treatment and prevention choices, but willingness to use them does not establish readiness to begin. We examined readiness to start these options, associated factors and conditions for acceptance among people living with HIV and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)-service clients in Uganda. This cross-sectional study analysed 225 participants at Mildmay Hospital and Kajjansi Health Centre IV in central Uganda. Readiness meant preferring initiation immediately or within three months. Modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), including age-by-service-group interaction. Separate models examined informational, perceptual and financial factors, adjusting for service group, age and sex. Logistic marginal standardisation checked demographic and expanded age comparisons. Overall, 108 participants (48.0%) were ready to start injectable HIV treatment or prevention, 111 (49.3%) wanted more information about these options, and six (2.7%) preferred initiation in six to twelve months. Readiness was 80.8% among people living with HIV aged 15-24 years and 34.4% among those aged 25 years or older (aPR 2.35, 95% CI 1.63-3.38). Corresponding proportions among PrEP-service clients were 39.2% and 41.4% (aPR 0.95, 95% CI 0.60-1.50; interaction p=0.002). In separate adjusted models, clinic-staff information (aPR 1.94, 95% CI 1.42-2.66), belief in greater effectiveness (2.00, 1.43-2.80) and a one-point increase in benefit score (3.27, 2.36-4.55) were associated with higher readiness. A one-point increase in concern score (0.70, 0.60-0.80) and financial difficulty sometimes or more often (0.68, 0.48-0.96) were associated with lower readiness. Fewer side effects was the leading condition for accepting injectable HIV treatment or prevention across service and readiness groups. Nearly half of participants were ready to start, while a similar proportion wanted further information about injectable options. Programmes should assess intended initiation timing alongside willingness and address safety, appointment flexibility, privacy and affordability through counselling and service planning.

papers.title: Sex workers experiences of HIV prevention, healthcare access and mental health in the West Rand District, South Africa: a qualitative study
papers.abstract: Sex workers experience disproportionate HIV vulnerability, while access to prevention, healthcare and mental health support is shaped by economic, social and institutional conditions. This study explored sex workers experiences of HIV prevention, healthcare access and mental health in the West Rand District, South Africa. A qualitative descriptive-interpretive design was used. Twenty unique participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling: five completed individual semi-structured interviews and 15 different participants took part in two focus group discussions comprising seven and eight participants. Data were audio-recorded with permission, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarkes six-phase approach, with NVivo 15 used for data organisation. Six themes were developed: sex work as economic survival rather than simple choice; HIV prevention under unequal client power; healthcare access shaped by stigma, fear and confidentiality concerns; participant-reported mental health distress as part of everyday sex work; peer educators as trusted bridges to care; and the need for inclusive and differentiated support. Participants described substantial knowledge of condoms, HIV testing and pre-exposure prophylaxis, but their accounts indicated that prevention preferences were negotiated within income needs, client demands, safety concerns and disclosure risks. Participants also reported anxiety, stress, trauma-related experiences, depressive symptoms and substance use in relation to work and healthcare experiences; these reports were not clinical diagnoses. Peer educators were described as trusted sources of information, referral, emotional support and clinic navigation. Overall, the findings suggest that meaningful access extends beyond geographical availability and is shaped by confidentiality, dignity, economic opportunity costs and trusted relationships. The findings support consideration of integrated, differentiated and peer-linked approaches in district-level HIV, healthcare and mental health planning.

papers.title: Patterns and correlates of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis use among higher-risk men who have sex with men in the Jakarta Metropolitan Area, Indonesia
papers.abstract: BackgroundMen who have sex with men (MSM) in the Jakarta Metropolitan Area (JMA), Indonesia are disproportionately affected by HIV. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a viable strategy for addressing enduring HIV disparities, yet remains underutilized among MSM in the JMA. Patterns and influences of PrEP use may inform future intervention targets but have not been extensively studied in this context. MethodsGuided by the Andersens Behavioral Model for Health Services Use, the present study investigated multidimensional correlates of varied PrEP use patterns among 183 JMA-based MSM aged 18-51 (median age=29) and at elevated risk of HIV infection. The multinomial regression model identified factors associated with current PrEP use and some use in the past, compared with never use (reference category). ResultsIn the present study, 107 (58%) participants reported never use, 34 (19%) current use, and 42 (23%) some use of PrEP. Current PrEP use was negatively associated with HIV stigma and positively with perceived social support, online HIV information seeking, and sexualized drug use. Some PrEP use was negatively associated with HIV stigma and positively with online HIV information seeking. ConclusionsThe study findings provide support for the Andersen models emphasis on predisposing characteristics, enabling resources, and need factors when tailoring PrEP implementation for higher-risk MSM in the JMA. Addressing stigma, reinforcing social support and HIV knowledge, and integrating PrEP care within multiple health care systems appear viable avenues for improving PrEP adoption in this key population.

papers.title: Predictors of malaria prevention practices among HIV-positive patients attending an antiretroviral therapy clinic in Kampala, Uganda: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMalaria and HIV remain major causes of illness in sub-Saharan Africa, accounting for 94% of the global malaria burden and over two-thirds of the global HIV burden. HIV-related immunosuppression increases susceptibility to malaria, with a higher malaria burden of up to 47% and severe malaria complications compared to HIV-negative individuals. Socio-demographic factors, individual knowledge, attitude, and perception are recognized determinants of malaria prevention behaviours, but no study has modelled their combined contribution, and there is scant research on these factors among people living with HIV. We assessed the level of knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions towards malaria, and identified the predictors of malaria prevention practice among HIV-positive individuals in Kampala, Uganda. MethodsThis cross-sectional study enrolled 620 HIV-positive patients attending the ART clinic of China-Uganda Friendship Hospital, Naguru, selected by systematic random sampling. Data collection was conducted from 21st July 2025 to 18th August 2025 using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire that measured socio-demographic characteristics, knowledge, attitude, perception, and the practice of malaria prevention. Associations were assessed using Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis H, and Spearman correlation. The independent predictors of good malaria prevention practice were identified using binary logistic regression. ResultsParticipants had a mean age of 34.8 years, were predominantly female (68.9%), Baganda (38.1%) by tribe, and the majority had a secondary level of education(46.0%). Most had good knowledge of malaria (97.3%) and a positive attitude (90.5%), while 57.3% held a positive perception of malaria risk and prevention; only 62.6% reported good malaria prevention practice, and most prevention methods used were sleeping under a mosquito net (71.1 3%) and closing windows early in the evening (70.3%). In regression analysis, knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.198, 95% CI 1.03-1.40, p = 0.023) and attitude (AOR 1.101, 95% CI 1.04-1.17, p = 0.001) independently predicted good practice, while perception did not (AOR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96-1.04, p = 0.994). Scores of Attitude, perception, and malaria prevention practices varied significantly, though non-linearly, by education level, and were highest among non-educated participants. ConclusionsDespite near-universal knowledge and predominantly positive attitudes in this study, more than a third of HIV-positive participants did not practice adequate malaria prevention, and perception did not independently predict malaria prevention practice once knowledge and attitude were accounted for. Programmes seeking to close this know-do gap should pair health education with structural support for prevention tools rather than education alone. Trial registrationNot applicable. This is an observational study of an existing care population, not a healthcare intervention.
